intro: ものの concedes a fact and then reports that the result you would expect from it did not follow: "it is true that X, but Y". It belongs to writing and careful speech, and its tone is calm and matter-of-fact rather than surprised or annoyed. It is most often seen after a past verb: 買ったものの, 始めたものの.

skills.rule: X ものの Y: "although X is true, Y", where Y falls short of what X would lead you to expect; Y is a statement, never a request or a plan.
skills.explain:
ものの follows the plain form of verbs and i-adjectives (取ったものの, 高いものの). Na-adjectives take な or である (便利なものの), and nouns take である (学生であるものの). The set phrase とはいうものの means "that said" or "it may be X, but".

The first half is a fact the writer admits; the second half reports a result that goes against it, often a disappointing one: 免許は取ったものの、ほとんど運転していない. The two halves may have different subjects.

The main clause must describe a fact or a judgement. It cannot be a request, an order, an invitation or the speaker's intention: 高いけれど買ってください, never 高いものの買ってください. In conversation, けど or のに are more usual; ものの sounds written and slightly formal, which is exactly why it appears in reports, essays and news.
patterns: [plain verb, often た form] ものの
[na-adjective] な / である ものの

examples.jp: 免許[めんきょ]は取[と]った{ものの}、ほとんど運転[うんてん]していない。
examples.en: I got my driving licence, but I hardly ever drive.

examples.jp: 薬[くすり]を飲[の]んだ{ものの}、熱[ねつ]はなかなか下[さ]がらなかった。
examples.en: I took some medicine, but the fever just wouldn't come down.

examples.jp: 新[あたら]しいパソコンを買[か]った{ものの}、使[つか]い方[かた]がよく分[わ]からない。
examples.en: I bought a new computer, but I don't really know how to use it.

examples.jp: この店[みせ]は値段[ねだん]が高[たか]い{ものの}、いつも客[きゃく]でいっぱいだ。
examples.en: Although this shop is expensive, it is always full of customers.

examples.jp: 春[はる]とはいう{ものの}、まだ寒[さむ]い日[ひ]が続[つづ]いている。
examples.en: It may be spring, but the cold days are still going on.

examples.jp: 理論上[りろんじょう]は可能[かのう]である{ものの}、実現[じつげん]するのは難[むずか]しい。
examples.en: Although it is possible in theory, it would be difficult to put into practice.

contrast.note: のに is the spoken "even though" with surprise, regret or complaint: 約束したのに来なかった! ものの states the same kind of mismatch coolly, in a written register.
ので gives a reason and an expected result: 雨が降ったので中止になった. ものの is the opposite: the result is not what the fact would predict.
ながら(も) as "although" needs one subject and attaches to stems, adjectives and bare nouns (狭いながらも). ものの takes the full plain form and allows two subjects.

mistakes.bad: 少[すこ]し高[たか]い{ものの}、ぜひ買[か]ってください。
mistakes.good: 少[すこ]し高[たか]い{けれど}、ぜひ買[か]ってください。
mistakes.note: ものの cannot be followed by a request, order or intention; use けれど or が.

mistakes.bad: 彼[かれ]はまだ学生[がくせい]の{ものの}、もう会社[かいしゃ]を経営[けいえい]している。
mistakes.good: 彼[かれ]はまだ学生[がくせい]である{ものの}、もう会社[かいしゃ]を経営[けいえい]している。
mistakes.note: A noun takes である before ものの, not の.

mistakes.bad: 大雨[おおあめ]が降[ふ]った{ものの}、試合[しあい]は中止[ちゅうし]になった。
mistakes.good: 大雨[おおあめ]が降[ふ]った{ので}、試合[しあい]は中止[ちゅうし]になった。
mistakes.note: Cancellation is the expected result of heavy rain, so this is a reason: ので.

skills.tip: Read it as "I did X, but it didn't lead where you'd think". If the second half is a request or the expected outcome, ものの is wrong.
